title: Review: Resistance and I–V characteristics; Resistivity; EMF and internal resistance
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL08-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL03-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL03-uk1#t4 term and clue written for the game; EL08-1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL03-1#N.3a, EL03-uk1#N.6, EL04-1#N.10a, EL04-uk1#N.3, EL08-1#N.7a, EL03-1#N.11, EL03-uk1#N.10, EL04-1#N.6a, EL04-uk1#N.10, EL08-1#N.10, EL03-1#N.14a, EL03-uk1#N.3. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: emf
items.clue: Energy transferred to each coulomb of charge by the source.

items.label: Reverse bias
items.clue: Way round that gives only a tiny current: very high resistance.

items.label: NTC thermistor
items.clue: Semiconductor component whose resistance falls as temperature rises.

items.label: Short circuit
items.clue: Connection with R = 0, giving a very large current that heats the cell.

questions.stem: Predict first. What is the origin of the electrical resistance of a metal wire?

options.text: Free electrons collide with the vibrating lattice ions, transferring energy to them.
Some of the free electrons are absorbed by the metal atoms, so fewer leave than enter.
The electrons rub against the surface of the wire, like water flowing along a pipe.
The electrons bump into one another as they crowd through the wire.

questions.stem: A copper wire has a fixed pd across it. As it warms up, the current falls. A student explains: "Warming reduces the number of free electrons in the copper." Which correction is right?

options.text: The student is right: fewer free electrons means a smaller current.
The wire expands as it warms, so it is longer and has a higher resistance.
The number of free electrons hardly changes; the ions vibrate more, so collisions slow the electrons' flow.
Warming gives the electrons more energy, so they move faster and fewer pass each second.

questions.explanation: Correct. More ion vibration means more frequent collisions. With the same number of carriers moving along more slowly, the current falls: R has risen.

questions.stem: Wire X has resistance R and is made of a material of resistivity ρ. Wire Y is made of the same material at the same temperature, but it is half as long as X and has half the diameter of X. What are the resistance and the resistivity of wire Y?

options.text: resistance R, resistivity ρ
resistance 2R, resistivity ρ
resistance 2R, resistivity 2ρ
resistance R/8, resistivity ρ

questions.explanation: R ∝ length ÷ area: the length factor is ½ and the area factor is ¼, so R_Y = (½ ÷ ¼)R = 2R. Same material and temperature, so the same ρ.

questions.stem: A student plots R against length for a uniform wire of diameter 0.40 mm. The best-fit line has a gradient of 4.0 Ω m⁻¹ and crosses the R axis at 0.30 Ω. What is the resistivity of the wire?

options.text: 4.0 Ω m

questions.explanation: A = π(0.40 × 10⁻³)²/4 = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m². ρ = gradient × A = 4.0 × 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. The 0.30 Ω intercept (contact resistance) does not affect the gradient.

questions.stem: Cells P and Q have the same emf. P has a smaller internal resistance than Q. Each cell is connected in turn to the same lamp. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The lamp is equally bright with each, as both cells have the same emf.
The terminal pd is larger with P, as less pd is lost inside P.
The terminal pd is larger with Q, as more of the emf is across its resistance.
The current is the same with each, as the lamp alone sets the current.

questions.explanation: Current = emf/(R + r) is larger with P, but lost volts Ir is still smaller, so terminal pd = emf − Ir is larger and the lamp brighter.

questions.stem: A student investigates whether a length of metal wire obeys Ohm's law. At the highest currents, V/I is clearly larger than at low currents. What is the best change to the method?

options.text: Use a voltmeter with a higher resolution, so the pd readings are more precise.
Take each reading twice, once with the supply reversed, and average the results.
Extend the range to even higher currents, so that more points lie on the graph.
Keep currents small or use a water bath, so the wire's temperature is constant.

questions.explanation: Ohm's law applies at constant temperature. Small currents (or a water bath) stop the wire heating, so V/I stays constant for an ohmic wire.

questions.stem: An NTC thermistor senses the temperature inside a fridge. After the door is closed, the thermistor cools from 15 °C to 5 °C. What happens to its resistance, and why?

options.text: It falls, because its ions vibrate less, so the carriers collide with them less often.
It rises, because fewer charge carriers are freed, outweighing the fewer collisions.
It rises, because its ions vibrate more as it cools, so there are more collisions.
It does not change, because a component's resistance is fixed when it is made.

questions.explanation: Cooling a semiconductor frees far fewer charge carriers. This outweighs the drop in collisions, so the resistance of an NTC thermistor rises.

questions.stem: A copper cable has length 5.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm. The resistivity of copper is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What is the resistance of the cable?
A cable is made from a ceramic superconductor with a critical temperature of 92 K. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It needs liquid helium (4 K), since every superconductor must be close to absolute zero.
Liquid nitrogen (77 K) keeps it superconducting, so it can carry a current with no heating.
It superconducts at room temperature, since 92 is well above zero.
At 77 K its resistivity is very small but not zero, so it still heats slightly.

questions.explanation: Right. 77 K is below 92 K, so its resistivity is zero: no energy is transferred as heat, however large the current.

questions.stem: A battery of internal resistance r is connected to an external resistor whose resistance equals r. The external resistor is then replaced by one of resistance 2r. How does the potential difference across the terminals of the battery change?

options.text: It stays equal to its first value.
It rises to 2 times its first value.
It falls to 2/3 of its first value.
It increases to 4/3 of its first value.

questions.stem: Three components X, Y and Z are tested. The currents at pds of 1.0 V, 2.0 V and 4.0 V are: X — 0.10 A, 0.20 A, 0.40 A; Y — 0.05 A, 0.15 A, 0.35 A; Z — 0.20 A, 0.30 A, 0.40 A. Which of the components are ohmic, and why?

options.text: X and Y: each gives a straight-line graph of I against V.
None of them: V/I should double as V doubles, and does not.
X only: V/I has the same value at every reading.
X, Y and Z: V = IR applies to every one of the readings.

questions.stem: The pd across a forward-biased silicon diode is raised from 0.2 V to 0.8 V. What happens to its resistance?

options.text: It rises, as in a filament lamp, because the diode warms up.
It stays constant, because once the diode conducts its graph is a straight line.
It falls to zero, so above 0.6 V the diode acts like a plain wire.
It falls a lot: almost no current at 0.2 V, a large current at 0.8 V.

questions.explanation: Below the threshold the current is tiny, so V/I is huge. Above it the current is large, so V/I is small.
